scope: Six original AQA AS 7408 3.1.2 uncertainty graph drawing and interpretation exercises requiring the learner's actual sketch
notes: Explicit numerical cases are independently checkable, but image/graph marks start unticked, never inferred from typed prose. The learner draws or photographs their graph then reviews mark points manually; not official AQA paper items or automatic graph recognition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Plot vertical uncertainty bars and a best-fit line
questions.prompt: Using a blank grid, plot displacement s / m against time t / s for the measurements (t, s ± absolute uncertainty): (0, 1.0 ± 0.2), (1, 3.0 ± 0.2), (2, 5.0 ± 0.2), (3, 7.0 ± 0.2). Show vertical error bars, draw a straight line of best fit and calculate its gradient with units. Review the graph manually. [5 marks]
markPoints: Axes labelled time t / s horizontally and displacement s / m vertically, with a sensible linear scale.
All four data points plotted at their given coordinates.
Each point has a vertical error bar extending 0.2 m above and 0.2 m below its central s value.
A single straight line of best fit follows the data (approximately s = 1.0 + 2.0t), not disconnected point-to-point segments.
Gradient evaluated from two well-spaced points ON the fit line: (7−1)/(3−0) = 2.0 m s⁻¹ (or an equivalent pair and correct units).
questions.modelAnswer: Use horizontal t / s and vertical s / m axes. Plot (0,1), (1,3), (2,5), (3,7), all with vertical bars ±0.2 m. A best-fit line s≈1+2t runs through the central points. For example its gradient is (7−1)/(3−0)=2.0 m s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Draw horizontal uncertainty bars
questions.prompt: Measurements have uncertain times but negligible uncertainty in distance. On a grid plot distance d / m vertically against time t / s horizontally for (t ± uncertainty, d): (1.0 ± 0.1, 4.0), (2.0 ± 0.1, 7.0), (3.0 ± 0.1, 10.0). Draw the appropriate error bars with scale and units. Review your sketch manually. [4 marks]
markPoints: Time t / s is the horizontal axis and distance d / m the vertical axis, both sensibly scaled.
All three central points at (1.0,4.0), (2.0,7.0), and (3.0,10.0) are plotted.
Each uncertainty bar runs HORIZONTALLY from t−0.1 s to t+0.1 s through the central data point.
No vertical uncertainty is invented: the stated uncertainty is only in the horizontal time readings.
questions.modelAnswer: Plot x=t / s and y=d / m. Points are (1,4), (2,7), (3,10). The first horizontal bar spans t=0.9 to 1.1 s; the second 1.9 to 2.1 s; the third 2.9 to 3.1 s. Do not use vertical bars here.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Best and shallowest feasible gradient
questions.prompt: Draw y against x (both arbitrary units) using (x, y ± uncertainty): (0, 1.0 ± 0.3), (2, 3.0 ± 0.3), (4, 5.0 ± 0.3), (6, 7.0 ± 0.3). Add vertical error bars, a central best-fit line, and the shallowest straight line consistent with EVERY uncertainty bar. Use your two gradients to find the percentage uncertainty in the best gradient. Show working and review the drawing manually. [6 marks]
markPoints: Suitable labelled and scaled x and y axes with all four central data points.
Vertical ±0.3 uncertainty bars correctly plotted at all four x positions.
Best-fit line drawn through the central trend, with gradient 1.0 (approximately y=1+x).
Shallowest permissible straight line touches the upper end of the first bar and lower end of the last (for example y=1.3+0.9x), while remaining inside both middle error bars.
Worst-case gradient calculated (6.7−1.3)/(6−0)=0.9, with a clear gradient triangle or working.
Percentage uncertainty calculated as |1.0−0.9|/1.0 ×100 = 10%.
questions.modelAnswer: Fit y=1+x (gradient 1.0). A shallow extreme line y=1.3+0.9x runs from (0,1.3) to (6,6.7), and at x=2,4 gives 3.1 and 4.9, inside the ±0.3 bars. Worst gradient=0.9; gradient percentage uncertainty=10%. Steepest line is also physically possible but use the stated shallowest case.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Uncertainty in a graph intercept
questions.prompt: Plot the readings (x, y ± uncertainty): (0, 2.0 ± 0.2), (2, 3.0 ± 0.2), (4, 4.0 ± 0.2), (6, 5.0 ± 0.2) on a graph of y against x. Draw the central best-fit line and a feasible worst-case straight line giving the smallest y-intercept. Estimate the absolute and percentage uncertainties in the central y-intercept. Review your drawing manually. [5 marks]
markPoints: Data and four vertical error bars of ±0.2 plotted on correctly labelled linear axes.
Central best-fit line y=2.0+0.5x drawn, with y-intercept 2.0.
Feasible extreme line passes through y=1.8 at x=0 and stays within all error bars (for example y=1.8+(3.4/6)x).
Absolute difference in intercepts is |2.0−1.8|=0.2 y units.
Percentage intercept uncertainty is (0.2/2.0)×100=10%.
questions.modelAnswer: Best line y=2+0.5x has intercept 2.0. A permissible minimum-intercept line joins (0,1.8) to (6,5.2): y=1.8+(3.4/6)x. It passes through all error bars. Absolute intercept uncertainty is 0.2; percentage uncertainty is 10%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Plot two-direction measurement uncertainty
questions.prompt: A single measured coordinate is x=(2.0 ± 0.1) s, y=(6.0 ± 0.5) m. On labelled axes draw the central data point and represent BOTH component measurement uncertainties accurately. State the end coordinates of each uncertainty bar. Review the plotted answer manually. [4 marks]
markPoints: Axes are correctly labelled x (s) and y (m), and the central point is plotted at (2.0, 6.0).
Horizontal uncertainty bar centred on x=2.0 spans x=1.9 s to x=2.1 s at y=6.0 m.
Vertical uncertainty bar centred on y=6.0 spans y=5.5 m to y=6.5 m at x=2.0 s.
Both error bars cross at the central reading and are parallel to their respective axes (not diagonal).
questions.modelAnswer: At coordinate (2.0 s,6.0 m), draw horizontal x bar from (1.9,6.0) to (2.1,6.0) and vertical y bar from (2.0,5.5) to (2.0,6.5). Label units on axes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Uncertainty and Practical Graphs
questions.question: Force-extension gradient with SI conversion
questions.prompt: For a spring in its linear region, measured extension e / mm and applied force F / N are (0, 0.0), (5, 1.0), (10, 2.0), (15, 3.0), (20, 4.0). Force uncertainty at each point is ±0.1 N; extension uncertainty is negligible. Plot F against e with error bars and a line of best fit. Use the gradient to find the spring constant in N m⁻¹. Review your graph manually. [5 marks]
markPoints: Axes are correctly identified and labelled extension e / mm horizontally and force F / N vertically.
All five central force–extension coordinates plotted, with vertical uncertainty bars ±0.1 N.
Straight best-fit line drawn through the central linear trend, close to the origin.
Gradient from distant points, for example (4.0−0.0)/(20−0)=0.20 N mm⁻¹.
Correct unit conversion gives k=0.20×1000=200 N m⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Plot F / N vertically and e / mm horizontally. Draw all five points and vertical ±0.1 N bars. Best-fit line is F≈0.20e when e is in mm. Gradient 0.20 N mm⁻¹ = 200 N m⁻¹, equal to the spring constant.
